title: Meaning and Scope of Accounting
outcomes: Explain what accounting is, how its definition widened from record-keeping to communication of information for decisions, and why it is called the language of business.
Describe the six stages of the accounting procedure and the objectives and functions of accounting.
Trace the evolution of accounting from ancient times through Pacioli to social responsibility accounting, and justify treating it as a social science.
Distinguish book-keeping from accounting and name the sub-fields of accounting.
Identify the internal and external users of accounting information and what each needs.
Explain the links between accounting and economics, statistics, mathematics, law and management, the limitations of accounting, and the services an accountant renders to society.

meta.exam_tip: Theory questions from this unit (book-keeping vs accounting, users, limitations, relationship with other disciplines) are regular 4–5 mark items. Answer in points or tables with one example each.

concepts.title: Transactions, events and why we keep accounts
body: Every person and organisation — a household, a club, a shop, a company, a municipal body, the government — carries on economic activity. That activity happens through transactions (dealings such as buying, selling, paying, borrowing) and events (results that follow from transactions, such as a profit for the year or goods remaining in stock).

Anyone running such an activity wants to know its result and position, and to decide what to do next. Accounting grew up to meet exactly this need: it measures inflows and outflows of economic resources and turns them into information for decisions. Because it is the common medium through which business results are conveyed, accounting is called the language of business.

head: Item
Transaction or event?
Reason
rows: An exchange/agreement between Ritu and her business
Goods worth ₹25,000 still in hand on 31 May
A result (a position) that follows from the purchases and sales
The outcome of all the month's transactions
blocks.title: Transactions versus events

concepts.analogy: A cricket match is made of balls bowled (transactions); the score at the end of an over or the result of the match is an event. You need the ball-by-ball record to know the result.
concepts.work: When a CA starts a new engagement, the first question is: which transactions and events of this client must be captured, and from which documents? Missing a category (say, credit card sales) means the result you report is wrong.

concepts.title: Meaning of accounting — from record-keeping to communication
body: Early definition (AICPA Committee on Terminology, 1961): accounting was described as an art — the art of putting on record, grouping and condensing, in money terms, those transactions and events which are at least partly financial, and then interpreting what they show. It treats accounting mainly as record keeping that ends with interpretation.

Wider definition (American Accounting Association, 1966): accounting is the process of identifying, measuring and communicating economic information so that users can make informed judgements and decisions. Communication was added because ownership and management separated, business became global and society took more interest in enterprises.
APB (AICPA), 1970, stated the function of accounting as providing quantitative, mainly financial, information about economic entities that is useful for economic decisions.

Working definition: accounting is the process of recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and interpreting financial transactions and communicating the results to persons interested in them. Only items measurable in money and of a financial character are recorded — opening a new bank branch is not recorded, but the business it brings in is.
concepts.analogy: Old view: a diary-writer who records and comments. Modern view: a news reporter who also has to make sure the right audience gets the story in a form it can use.
concepts.work: Clients rarely ask a CA for "books"; they ask "can I afford this loan?" or "why did profit fall?". The modern definition — information for decisions — is what the profession is paid for.

concepts.title: Procedure, objectives and functions of accounting
body: Procedure — generating information: (1) recording in the journal or subsidiary books, from documents such as bills, pass books, salary slips; (2) classifying into ledger accounts; (3) summarising into financial statements. Using information: (4) analysing — methodically regrouping the figures and establishing relationships; (5) interpreting — explaining what the relationships mean, why things happened and what may happen; (6) communicating — sending reports, ratios, graphs and statements to users.

Objectives: systematic recording of transactions; ascertaining the result (profit or loss) through the profit and loss account; ascertaining the financial position through the balance sheet; providing information to users for rational decisions; and knowing the liquidity (short-run) and solvency (long-run) position.

Functions: measurement of past performance and present position; forecasting; decision-making; comparison and evaluation against targets; control (spotting weaknesses and checking that corrective steps work); and supporting government regulation and taxation.

head: Stage
What Sahil Caterers does
Book / output
rows: Enters each catering bill, supplier invoice and wage slip in date order
Collects all wage payments under one head, all gas bills under another, and so on
Prepares the trial balance and then the profit and loss account and balance sheet

Explains why food cost rose from 38% to 45% of sales and what it means for profit

blocks.title: Generating and using financial information
blocks.note: Stages 1–2 (with the trial balance) are book-keeping; stages 3–6 are accounting proper.

concepts.analogy: A doctor's visit: recording symptoms, sorting them, summarising in a report, analysing test results, interpreting the diagnosis and finally explaining it to the patient.
concepts.work: In month-end closing at a company, accountants record and classify (book-keeping); the finance manager summarises and analyses; the CFO interprets and communicates to the board. Knowing which stage you are responsible for tells you what output is expected of you.

concepts.title: Evolution of accounting as a social science
body: History: around 4000 BC Egyptian treasury keepers sent daily reports to Wazirs and monthly reports to the king; Babylonia used accounts to detect losses from fraud and inefficiency; Greece used them to divide revenue among treasuries; Rome kept memorandum or day books of receipts and payments (700 BC–400 AD); China had advanced government accounting by about 2000 BC. In India, Kautilya's Arthashastra described how records should be kept.

Luca Pacioli, a Franciscan friar, published Summa de Arithmetica, Geometria, Proportioni et Proportionalita in Venice in 1494 — regarded as the first printed book on double-entry book-keeping. Debit comes from the Italian debito (Latin debere — owed), credit from credito (Latin credo — trust or belief).

Phases: (1) stewardship accounting — stewards accounting to wealthy owners, the root of financial accounting; (2) financial accounting — joint stock companies separated ownership from management, so law required disclosure of the profit and loss account and balance sheet to protect investors; (3) management accounting — a 20th-century development serving management decisions; (4) social responsibility accounting — still forming, it aims to report the social costs (pollution, use of society's resources) and social benefits (employment, better products) of a business.

Why a social science: social sciences study people in society and the results of social relationships. Accounting is judged by its usefulness to society as a whole — it produces information for social good, contributes to social progress and keeps changing as society changes.
concepts.analogy: Like language itself: it began as simple tally marks for a few people and grew, as society grew, into a shared system everyone relies on.
concepts.work: Today's sustainability and CSR reports that listed companies publish are the modern face of social responsibility accounting; CAs are increasingly asked to prepare and assure them.

concepts.title: Book-keeping, accounting and accountancy; sub-fields
body: Book-keeping is the orderly recording of financial data — the procedural, record-keeping part. Its objectives are a complete, permanent record of all transactions and knowing their combined effect on the business. Recording and classifying (with the trial balance) are book-keeping; preparing, analysing, interpreting and communicating financial statements are accounting. Accounting starts where book-keeping ends. Accountancy is the widest term, containing accounting, which in turn contains book-keeping.

Legal angle: companies keep books and prepare statements under the Companies Act; banks and insurers under their special Acts. There is no specific statute prescribing books or formats for sole proprietors and partnership firms. (Write this in the exam. In practice, tax laws — income-tax and GST — do require many such businesses and professionals to keep books and records, but they do not lay down a format for the financial statements.)

Sub-fields: financial accounting (historical; ends in the profit and loss account and balance sheet), management accounting (internal reports for planning, control and decisions), cost accounting (ascertaining and controlling costs), social responsibility accounting (social costs and benefits) and human resource accounting (identifying, valuing and reporting the investment in people, which conventional accounts ignore).

The base on which accounting rests

concepts.analogy: Book-keeping is collecting and labelling the ingredients; accounting is cooking the meal, tasting it and serving it; accountancy is the whole kitchen.
concepts.work: Data-entry staff or software do most book-keeping today; employers hire CAs for the accounting part — judgement, analysis and communication. That is why your training focuses on the "why" behind every entry.

concepts.title: Users of accounting information
body: Internal users: management (owners, directors, managers, partners) who use detailed, often confidential reports for decisions; employees are usually also counted as internal in the sense that they work inside the business.

External users rely on published financial statements: investors (buy, hold or sell; ability to pay dividends; owners of non-corporate firms decide whether to continue), lenders (repayment of principal and interest), suppliers and creditors (ability to pay; credit terms), customers (continuity of supply), government and its agencies (regulation, resource allocation, price control, taxes) and the public (contribution to the local economy).
Useful information stresses economic substance over technical form, is relevant, material and unbiased, and lets users judge its reliability and compare it with alternatives and past experience.

head: User
Internal / external
What they want to know from the accounts of Nimbus Foods Ltd
rows: Which product line earns most, whether to open a new plant, where costs can be cut
Is the company stable enough to pay salaries, bonus and retirement benefits and to grow jobs?
Should we buy, hold or sell the shares? Can the company keep paying dividends?
Will interest and the loan principal be repaid on time?
Can the company pay our bills? How much credit, at what terms?
Will the company keep supplying us — is it likely to survive?
Tax payable, compliance with regulations, data for policy
Local employment, purchases from local suppliers, environmental impact
blocks.title: Users of accounting information

concepts.analogy: One set of accounts is like one X-ray seen by several specialists — each looks for what matters to their own decision.
concepts.work: Before a bank sanctions a loan, its credit team reads the borrower's statements; before a vendor gives 60 days' credit, it asks for the latest balance sheet. CAs prepare statements knowing who will read them and what they will look for.

concepts.title: Relationship with other disciplines and limitations of accounting
body: Accounting overlaps economics, statistics, mathematics, law and management. A good accountant needs working knowledge of each, to use it directly or to know when to seek expert advice.

Limitations: (1) factors that cannot be measured in money — staff skill and loyalty — are left out; (2) the balance sheet shows the position on one date, while users want the future; (3) changes in the value of money (inflation) are ignored; (4) accounting principles sometimes conflict; (5) many figures rest on personal judgement — provision for doubtful debts, depreciation method, capital vs revenue, inventory valuation method; (6) human resources are not shown as assets for lack of an accepted valuation formula; (7) alternative policies for the same item open the door to manipulation — standards reduce, but cannot eliminate, the options.

head: Discipline
How it connects with accounting
rows: Both deal with scarce resources and decisions. Accountants borrowed ideas of value, income and capital from economists but made them workable — e.g. an asset is recorded at acquisition cost instead of the present value of all its future earnings, which cannot be estimated reliably. Accounting data of firms (micro) add up to the national (macro) data economists use.

Accounts are exact to the paisa; decisions often need only approximations, averages and trends. Ratios, time-series and cross-section comparisons and models that predict sickness of a firm rest on statistical methods applied to accounting data.

Double entry can be written algebraically. Interest, annuities, depreciation, instalments, lease rentals, sinking funds and ratios all need arithmetic and algebra; computers allow matrix methods; graphs need geometry.

Transactions are governed by the Contract Act, Sale of Goods Act, Negotiable Instruments Act, etc. The Companies Act prescribes the format of company financial statements; banks, insurers and electricity companies follow their own Acts. Law shapes accounting, and accounting knowledge shapes the law.
Much accounting information is produced for management decisions; accountants sit in the management team and design the system to serve its needs.

concepts.analogy: A photograph is accurate about the moment it was taken, but it cannot show what happens next or how the people in it feel. Financial statements have the same strengths and blind spots.
concepts.work: An analyst reading two companies' results first checks their accounting policies (depreciation, inventory) — the limitation "different policies for the same item" can make one company look better simply because of a choice of method.

concepts.title: Role of the accountant in society
body: The profession is respected because it serves the public interest — turning silent figures into information that helps businesses plan and society progress. Goethe is said to have called it one of the finest inventions of the human mind.

Areas of service: maintenance of books of account; statutory audit (every company must appoint a CA or a firm of CAs to report whether the statements give a true and fair view; co-operatives and others under their laws or by choice); internal audit (reviewing systems, safeguards against leakage and misappropriation, and efficiency); taxation (compliance, representation before authorities, planning, and views on tax policy); management accounting and consultancy (MIS, cost control, investment appraisal, working capital, corporate planning); financial advice (investments, insurance, business expansion and mergers, investigations — e.g. why profits fell, whether fraud occurred, valuing a business or shares — and pension schemes); and other services such as secretarial work, share registration, company formation, receiverships and liquidations, and arbitration.
concepts.analogy: A CA is like a family doctor for money matters — routine check-ups (books, audit), specialist treatment (tax, investigations) and advice on healthy habits (planning).
concepts.work: A typical small CA practice does all of these in a single week: GST returns for a trader, tax audit for a doctor, internal audit of a hospital, a valuation for a family settlement and advice on a startup's fund-raising.

illustrations.title: Spotting transactions and events, and finding the surplus
illustrations.q: Ritu opened Ritu Mobile Accessories on 1 May 2026 with ₹3,00,000 of her own money. During May she bought goods for ₹1,80,000, sold goods for ₹2,10,000, paid shop rent ₹8,000 and electricity ₹2,000. On 31 May goods costing ₹25,000 remained unsold. (a) Classify the items as transactions or events. (b) Work out the surplus for May.

head: Item
Transaction or event?
Reason
rows: An exchange/agreement between Ritu and her business
Goods worth ₹25,000 still in hand on 31 May
A result (a position) that follows from the purchases and sales
The outcome of all the month's transactions
solution.title: Transactions versus events

head: Particulars
Amount (₹)
rows: Add: Goods still lying in the shop on 31 May
solution.title: Statement of surplus — Ritu Mobile Accessories, May 2026
Why the unsold goods are added
solution.text: Goods bought (₹1,80,000) are charged in full, so the goods still in hand (₹25,000) are added back — otherwise the cost of unsold goods would reduce May's result. Surplus = 2,10,000 + 25,000 − 1,80,000 − 8,000 − 2,000 = ₹45,000.
The ₹3,00,000 brought in by Ritu is capital, not income, so it does not enter the surplus.

checks.label: Surplus of Ritu Mobile Accessories for May
Value of goods sold plus goods still in hand

jobs.title: Explaining the accounts to a first-time borrower
jobs.role: Article assistant at a CA firm, supporting a loan application for a small manufacturer
jobs.situation: Mr. Bansal runs a small packaging unit. The bank has asked for audited statements and projections. He asks you: "My books are written up every day by my clerk — why do I need you?"
steps: Explain that his clerk does book-keeping — recording and classifying — and that the bank needs accounting: summarised statements, analysis and interpretation.
List what the bank (a lender) will look for: ability to repay principal and interest, liquidity, and the trend in profit.
Point out limitations he should be ready to explain: figures based on estimates (depreciation, doubtful debts) and items not in the books (his skilled staff, a long-standing customer base).
Prepare a short covering note that communicates the key numbers in plain words with a simple chart.
jobs.takeaway: Book-keeping produces data; accounting turns it into information a particular user can act on. The CA adds the summarising, analysis, interpretation and communication.
jobs.think: Which two objectives of accounting matter most to the bank in this case?
jobs.answer: Ascertaining the financial position (balance sheet) and knowing the liquidity and solvency position — the bank wants to know whether the loan can be repaid.

jobs.title: Choosing what to report to different users
jobs.role: Junior accountant in the finance team of a listed company
jobs.situation: The CFO asks you to draft two reports from the same quarter's data: one for the board and one summary for publication.
steps: For the board (internal users): product-wise margins, department costs, budget versus actual, cash forecasts — detailed and confidential.
For publication (external users): the statutory statements and key disclosures — summarised, in the prescribed format, without sensitive internal detail.
Check that both reports agree with the same ledger data so that the story told is consistent.
jobs.takeaway: Internal users get detailed management reports; external users get structured financial statements. Same data, different presentation.

mcqs.q: Which definition of accounting added "communicating" economic information to permit informed judgements and decisions?
mcqs.explain: The 1961 AICPA definition ended with interpreting; the 1966 AAA definition described accounting as identifying, measuring and communicating information for users' decisions.

mcqs.q: The book in which classified information is kept under separate account heads is the:
mcqs.explain: Recording is done in the journal; classification into account heads is done in the ledger.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an event rather than a transaction?
mcqs.explain: Purchases, payments and borrowings are transactions; the profit for the year is a result of them — an event.

mcqs.q: The first printed book on double-entry book-keeping was written by:
mcqs.explain: Pacioli's Summa de Arithmetica (Venice, 1494) contains the first printed treatment of double entry.

mcqs.q: Management accounting as a branch of accounting is a development of the:
mcqs.explain: Stewardship came first, then financial accounting with joint stock companies; management accounting developed in the 20th century.

mcqs.q: Accounting is treated as a social science mainly because:
options: Its usefulness to society as a whole is the basic test of its worth
It is exact to the last paisa
It is governed by the Companies Act
mcqs.explain: Social sciences study people in society; accounting generates information for social good and adapts to social change.

mcqs.q: Which statement about book-keeping is correct?
options: It is the recording phase and provides the base for accounting
It includes preparation and interpretation of financial statements
It has several sub-fields such as cost accounting
Management decisions are taken directly from book-keeping records
mcqs.explain: Book-keeping is the recording phase; statements, interpretation, sub-fields and decision support belong to accounting.

mcqs.q: Lenders are mainly interested in accounting information to know:
options: Whether principal and interest will be repaid when due
The rate of dividend to be declared
The local contribution of the enterprise
mcqs.explain: Lenders want repayment of loan and interest on time; dividends concern investors; local contribution concerns the public.

mcqs.q: The attempt to identify, quantify and report the investment made in an organisation's people is called:
mcqs.explain: Human resource accounting deals with investment in human resources, which conventional accounts ignore.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a limitation of accounting?
options: It ignores changes in the purchasing power of money
It records transactions in money terms
It is based on documentary evidence
mcqs.explain: Inflation is ignored; recording in money and using documents are features, and profit ascertainment is an objective.

mcqs.q: Every company must appoint a chartered accountant (or a firm) to report on whether its financial statements give a true and fair view. This service is:
mcqs.explain: Statutory audit is required by law; internal audit is a management tool; investigation is done for a specific purpose.

mcqs.q: Statistical methods are used with accounting data mainly because:
options: Decisions often need trends and averages rather than exact individual figures
Accounting covers a period longer than statistics
The Companies Act requires statistical formats
mcqs.explain: Accounts are precise, but decision-making often needs only broad generalisations, averages and trends over longer periods.

model.text: In short, book-keeping provides the data and accounting starts where book-keeping ends. Accountancy is the wider body of knowledge that contains both.

scheme.pt: Book-keeping is the base; accounting begins where book-keeping ends / language of business
Financial statements and financial position come from accounting, not book-keeping
Decisions taken on accounting reports; book-keeping records alone do not support them
Sub-fields exist only in accounting (financial, management, cost etc.); answer presented as a table

remarks: Most candidates give two or three points and stop; five distinct bases are needed for five marks.
Points written as "book-keeping is narrow, accounting is wide" without explanation earn little.
mistakes: Treating the two terms as synonyms.
Putting the trial balance under accounting instead of book-keeping.
Writing the same idea twice in different words.
tips: Use a three-column table: Basis | Book-keeping | Accounting.
One mark per clear basis — aim for five or six bases.

questions.q: "Accounting is the language of business, but like every language it has its limitations." Explain any four limitations of accounting.

items: Items not measurable in money — the skill, loyalty and morale of staff or the reputation of the management — are not recorded, even though they may be the most valuable resources of the business.
Historical and dated: the balance sheet shows the position on one particular date, while users want to judge the near and long-term future.
Ignores changes in the value of money: assets bought in different years at different price levels are added together as if a rupee were always worth the same.
Subjectivity: depreciation method, provision for doubtful debts, inventory valuation and the capital/revenue split depend on the accountant's judgement, so two accountants can show different profits.
Alternative policies for the same item increase the chance of manipulation; Accounting Standards reduce the choices but cannot bring them down to one.
Accounting principles sometimes conflict with one another.

model.text: Hence financial statements should be read carefully, keeping these factors in mind.

scheme.pt: Non-monetary factors (e.g. human resources) not recorded
Position on a past date — not the future
Inflation / changing value of money ignored
Personal judgement or alternative policies / conflicting principles (any one, explained)

remarks: Answers that only list headings without a line of explanation are awarded half marks per point.
Good answers give an example for each limitation, such as depreciation method for subjectivity.
mistakes: Writing objectives or functions of accounting instead of limitations.
Giving "it is time-consuming" or "it is costly" — these are not the limitations the examiner is looking for.
tips: Number each limitation and bold the key phrase.
Close with one line on why users must interpret statements carefully.

questions.q: Explain the relationship of accounting with (a) economics, (b) statistics, (c) mathematics, (d) law and (e) management.

How it connects with accounting
rows: Both deal with scarce resources and decisions. Accountants borrowed ideas of value, income and capital from economists but made them workable — e.g. an asset is recorded at acquisition cost instead of the present value of all its future earnings, which cannot be estimated reliably. Accounting data of firms (micro) add up to the national (macro) data economists use.

Double entry can be written algebraically. Interest, annuities, depreciation, instalments, lease rentals, sinking funds and ratios all need arithmetic and algebra; computers allow matrix methods; graphs need geometry.

Transactions are governed by the Contract Act, Sale of Goods Act, Negotiable Instruments Act, etc. The Companies Act prescribes the format of company financial statements; banks, insurers and electricity companies follow their own Acts. scheme.pt: Economics: scarce resources/decisions; concepts of value, income, capital adapted (acquisition cost example); micro to macro data
Statistics: precision vs approximation; trends, ratios, comparisons
Mathematics: algebra of double entry; interest, annuity, depreciation, instalments
Law: transactions governed by laws; formats prescribed by Companies Act and special Acts; two-way influence
Management: accounting data as the base for management decisions; accountant in the management team

remarks: The economics part carries the most weight; the best answers mention the gap between the economist's and the accountant's idea of value with an example.
Many candidates write only "accounting uses law" — the two-way influence is what earns the full mark.
mistakes: Writing a general essay on each subject without linking it to accounting.
Leaving out management, which is the easiest mark.
tips: Use sub-headings (a) to (e) — examiners award marks part by part.
Give one concrete example under each discipline.

summary: Accounting: recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating financial information for users' decisions — the language of business.
Definitions: AICPA 1961 (art of recording … interpreting), AAA 1966 (identifying, measuring, communicating), APB 1970 (quantitative information useful for economic decisions).

Objectives: record, find result (P&L), find position (balance sheet), inform users, know liquidity/solvency. Functions: measurement, forecasting, decision-making, comparison & evaluation, control, government regulation & taxation.
Evolution: stewardship → financial → management (20th century) → social responsibility accounting. Pacioli, Venice, 1494. Social science because it serves society.
Book-keeping = recording phase; accounting begins where it ends. Sub-fields: financial, management, cost, social responsibility, human resource accounting.
Users: internal (management, employees) and external (investors, lenders, suppliers, customers, government, public).
remember: Trial balance is still book-keeping; financial statements are accounting.
No specific law prescribes books for sole proprietors and partnership firms; companies, banks and insurers have their Acts.
Seven limitations: non-monetary items, past date, inflation, conflicting principles, judgement, human resources, alternative policies.
traps: Do not call profit for the year a transaction — it is an event.
Do not confuse internal audit (management tool) with statutory audit (required by law).
Do not say standards eliminate all alternative treatments — they only reduce them.

viva.model: Users are internal, like management and employees, and external, like investors, lenders, suppliers, customers, government and the public. Lenders want to know whether the principal and interest will be repaid on time. Investors want to decide whether to buy, hold or sell and whether the business can pay dividends.

points.pt: Internal users: management, employees
External users: investors, lenders, suppliers, customers, government, public
Lenders: repayment of principal and interest on time
Investors: buy, hold or sell; ability to pay dividends

viva.q: Why is accounting called a social science, and what are the phases of its evolution?
viva.model: Accounting is a social science because its usefulness to society as a whole is the test of its value; it produces information for social good and changes as society changes. It evolved from stewardship accounting to financial accounting with joint stock companies, then management accounting in the twentieth century, and now social responsibility accounting.

points.pt: Usefulness to society / social good is the basic test
Stewardship accounting came first
Financial accounting with joint stock companies
Management accounting, then social responsibility accounting

viva.q: State any four limitations of accounting.
viva.model: First, things that cannot be measured in money, like the skill and loyalty of staff, are not recorded. Second, the balance sheet shows the position on a past date, not the future. Third, accounting ignores inflation, that is changes in the value of money. Fourth, many figures depend on personal judgement and different accounting policies can be chosen, which allows manipulation.

points.pt: Non-monetary items (staff skill, loyalty, human resources) not recorded
kw: not record|not shown|not includ|ignor|left out|cannot|can t|exclud|not measur|not appear|no place

points.pt: Shows position on a past date, not the future
Ignores inflation / change in value of money
kw: inflation|price level|price change|purchasing power|value of money|changing value

points.pt: Personal judgement / estimates / alternative policies allow manipulation

viva.q: What services does a chartered accountant render to society?
viva.model: A chartered accountant maintains books of account, conducts statutory audit and internal audit, handles taxation matters including planning and representation, provides management accounting and consultancy, gives financial advice on investments, insurance, expansion and investigations, and does other work like company formation, liquidation and arbitration.

points.pt: Maintenance of books of account
Statutory audit and internal audit
Taxation
Management consultancy / financial advice / investigations, liquidation, arbitration etc.

cases.title: Green Leaf Organics — one set of accounts, many readers
cases.case: Green Leaf Organics Pvt Ltd sells packaged organic food. Its accountant enters every invoice and payment daily and posts them to ledger accounts. At the year end, the finance head prepares the profit and loss account and balance sheet, calculates ratios, explains why margins fell and sends a report to the directors and to the company's bank. A local NGO asks for the accounts to see how many farmers in the district supply the company. The directors also wonder whether to show the value of their highly trained team in the balance sheet.

mcqs.q: The daily entry of invoices and posting to ledger accounts is an example of:
mcqs.explain: Recording and classifying (up to the trial balance) form book-keeping; the later stages are accounting.

mcqs.q: Explaining why margins fell is which stage of the accounting procedure?
mcqs.explain: Interpreting explains the meaning and significance of the relationships found in analysis — why something happened.

mcqs.q: The NGO interested in the company's purchases from local farmers is best described as:
mcqs.explain: The public at large is interested in an enterprise's contribution to the local economy, such as local employment and patronage of local suppliers.

mcqs.q: Can the trained team be shown as an asset in the balance sheet under conventional accounting?
options: No — human resources cannot be measured reliably in money, which is a recognised limitation
Yes — at the salaries paid during the year
Yes — at a value fixed by the directors
No — because employees are external users
mcqs.explain: Conventional accounting records only items measurable in money; there is no generally accepted formula for valuing human resources. Human resource accounting is the sub-field that attempts it.
